what: Qualys sells cloud-based security software. It scans a company's servers, laptops, cloud accounts and web applications for known vulnerabilities and misconfigurations, prioritises what to fix and increasingly applies the patches itself.
customers: Security and IT operations teams at large and mid-sized companies, government agencies and regulated industries that must document their security posture for auditors.
money: Annual subscriptions to the cloud platform, priced by the number of assets scanned and the modules enabled.
moat: Vulnerability scanning is a compliance requirement, so the spending is non-discretionary. Qualys has been collecting vulnerability signatures for over two decades, and once its agents are deployed across thousands of machines, replacing them is a large project with no obvious benefit.
risks: Growth has slowed markedly: revenue rose from $607.6M in 2024 to $669.1M in 2025, well below the pace of earlier years.
Larger security platforms, CrowdStrike and Microsoft above all, are adding vulnerability management to suites customers already buy, which squeezes standalone vendors.
The shares trade at about 32 times earnings and 9.3 times sales, which requires growth to hold up.
The eighteen analysts average a $196.81 target, only about 2% above the current price, meaning the market and the analysts agree there is little upside priced in.
Customer counts have grown slowly, so revenue growth depends on selling more modules to existing customers.
opportunities: Profitability is unusual for a security software company: about 30% net margin and $324.4M of free cash flow on $721.1M of revenue.
The balance sheet carries only $52.3M of debt against $250.3M of cash, and the company buys back shares consistently.
Cloud and container security are newer modules that expand what each customer can be sold.
Compliance-driven demand is resilient in a downturn because auditors do not relax requirements when budgets tighten.
watch: Revenue growth rate. The profitability is excellent and well established; the only real question is whether growth stabilises in the low teens or continues to decelerate toward nothing.
